Full Terms & Conditions of access and use can be found at
            https://www.tandfonline.com/action/journalInformation?journalCode=rspb20
 SPORTS BIOMECHANICS
https://doi.org/10.1080/14763141.2025.2498338
RESEARCH ARTICLE
Training alters joint power distributions during running in
National Football League Draft Preparation Players
G. Monique Mokha, Marissa Bonsangue, ToniAnn Brezina and Jacob Haberer
Exercise and Sport Science, Nova Southeastern University, Fort Lauderdale, FL, USA
    ABSTRACT                                                                   ARTICLE HISTORY
    The aim of this study was to compare joint-specific contributions to       Received 4 October 2024
    total lower limb joint power during a speed run in American style          Accepted 23 April 2025
    football players before and after a 6-week National Football League        KEYWORDS
    (NFL) draft preparation camp. Fifty-two players performed one 5-           American style football; team
    second treadmill run at 5.5–6.5 m/s before and after camp. Speed           sport running; kinetics;
    was consistent between tests. Bilateral hip, knee, and ankle power         performance; joint power
    generation (positive) and absorption (negative) were calculated
    from kinematics and kinetics using inverse dynamics. Negative
    total limb power decreased for both limbs, significantly for the
    left (Z = −2.113, p = .035, r = .30) due to significant decreases in
    negative ankle power bilaterally (left, Z = −1.967, p = .049, r = .27;
    right, Z = −2.623, p = .009, r = .36). The contribution of negative left
    hip power significantly increased (Z = −2.398, p = .016, r = .31).
    While no other significant changes in positive or negative joint-
    specific magnitudes or contributions occurred, there were general
    distal-to-proximal shifts in joint power contributions. Players appear
    to have adopted more energy efficient running through moderate
    joint-specific mechanistic training adaptations such as a reduction
    in ankle power absorption.
Introduction
Sprint speed is a key skill for American style football players. Players seeking to be drafted
by the National Football League (NFL) showcase their linear speed running abilities in
the 36.6 m (40 yard) dash at an annual combine. The combine is a weeklong invitation-
only event where top university prospects (approximately 300) perform physical and
mental assessments for personnel of the league’s 32 teams. Research shows drafted
players perform better in the 36.6 m sprint than non-drafted players (Sierer et al.,
2008) and superior performance is associated with higher draft position (Tucker &
Black, 2023). Combine invitees and other eligible players attend specialised training
camps leading up to the NFL draft to prepare. Linear speed mechanics is one focus of
these camps since players must transition from game play running to test performance
running. Mokha et al. (2021) showed that 36.6 m time significantly improved in a group
of American style football players participating in a six-week NFL draft preparation
camp. Players appeared to accomplish this through decreasing ground contact time (pre,
177 ± 3.2 vs. post, 168 ± 2.2 ms) and increasing average vertical ground reaction force
CONTACT G. Monique Mokha                gm588@nova.edu
© 2025 International Society of Biomechanics in Sports
 2      G. M. MOKHA ET AL.
(vGRF) (pre, 1.5 ± 0.3 vs. post, 1.6 ± 0.1 BW). These changes represent hallmarks of
higher velocity runs (Colyer et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2011; Weyand, 2017; Weyand et al.,
2010). While these changes alone would not be enough to improve the participants’
linear speed in the 36.6 m dash, they shed light on how foot-ground kinetics are modifi­
able in elite American style football players and provide foundation for further kinetic
analysis.
    During running, mechanical work must be done to rotate limb segments, restore
energy lost during early ground contact, and propel the body forward. Given that ground
contact times for sprinting range from 85 to 190 ms (Mattes et al., 2021; Numella et al.,
2007; Weyand et al., 2010), the ability to perform work in a short time is vital and gives
rise to examining joint power. Decrements in the capacity of the muscles to produce
adequate power during running have been shown to negatively impact sprint speed
(Sánchez-Sánchez et al., 2018; Small et al., 2009). Joint power is distinguished from
system power where system power represents the rate at which the mechanical work is
done on an external load and may veil the power contributions from the individual joints
(Moir et al., 2012). Joint powers represent the rate at which mechanical work is accom­
plished at the joints providing estimates of muscle activity (Pires et al., 2014; Riddick &
Kuo, 2022). Joint power magnitudes have been shown to increase as running speeds
increase (Belli et al., 2002; Khassetarash et al., 2020). While improvements in speed and
system power performance have been documented in American style football players
undergoing training (Crawley et al., 2024; Gillen et al., 2024; Hoffman et al., 2004, 2009;
Moore & Fry, 2007), the joint level mechanisms underlying adaptation have not been
explored.
    Positive joint power is primarily generated by concentric muscle contractions and
potential strain energy is released. Most of the positive power (>60%) is generated at the
ankle joint during ground contact when the plantar flexors (gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles) contract to propel the body forward (Swinnen et al., 2021). Sanno et al. (2018)
reported that prolonged running at near maximal effort shifted the distribution of
positive joint work proximally in recreational but not competitive distance runners
suggesting that shifting positive joint work from the ankle plantar flexors towards hip
extensors could be detrimental to running economy. This shift has also been reported to
occur in middle-distance runners completing an exhaustive run (181 ± 42 s to exhaus­
tion) and in older runners as a sign of performance decline (Kim & Park, 2022).
Furthermore, hip muscle activation during the swing phase consumes energy, leading
to the estimated relative contribution of leg swing to the energetic cost of 7–11%
(Swinnen et al., 2021). While these findings appear to indicate that a distal-to-proximal
shift may be deleterious, it may be a necessary adaptation to faster running speeds. For
example, the hip’s contribution to average positive power in both stance and swing
phases has been shown to significantly increase with faster running speeds (i.e.,
6.0–9.0 m/s) (Schache et al., 2011, 2015). AminiAghdam et al. (2021) found that anterior
trunk lean shifted power from the knee to the hip during level and uneven running at
speeds of 3.5 m/s.
    Negative joint work and power are primarily generated by eccentric muscle contrac­
tions where potential strain energy is stored and mechanical energy is reduced (DeVita et
al., 2007). Since eccentric muscle contractions are associated with greater muscle damage
(Hashizume et al., 2017), negative joint power is of particular interest. Negative power is
                                                                  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       3
produced during the braking phase of running and is controlled reflexively by the leg
extensors (Belli et al., 2002). The knee and ankle joints contribute greatly to limb power
absorption compared to the hip joint (Hashizume et al., 2018). Belli et al. (2002) found
the overall negative work absorbed at initial contact was lower than the positive power
produced at end contact point, especially at the knee joint. The elongation time of the
ankle and knee muscles is short and has been attributed to high ankle joint stiffness
preventing yielding of the centre of mass at initial contact (Belli et al., 2002). It is not
known how participating in a performance preparation program affects this mechanism.
   Magnitudes and percentage contributions of joint power to total limb power may be
sensitive to training aimed at improving linear speed mechanics even in highly trained
athletes. Exploring joint level mechanics in American style football players may provide
insight into the mechanistic adaptations of running performance that may carry over to
other team sports where running is integral such as rugby, football (soccer), or Australian
rules football. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to assess the changes in joint
power magnitude and distribution during a high-speed run before and after a six-week
training camp in American style football players. We hypothesised that speed focused
exercises presented in training camp would redistribute the power contributions from
the lower limb joints, characterised by a reduction of power from the ankle even if
treadmill speed were kept uniform. To test the hypothesis, we used an inverse dynamic
approach to calculate individual joint and total limb powers during a high-speed run
before and after participation in training camp.
Materials and methods
Experimental approach
This study was part of a larger study monitoring pre-post changes in body composition,
and vertical jump and speed running mechanics over the duration of a six-week training
camp designed to prepare eligible American style football players for the NFL draft.
Camp was divided into three microcycles that included drill specificity training, player
position specificity training, resistance training and recovery-based movement (e.g.,
pool, soft tissue massage). The study procedures were conducted at the start of training
camp and six weeks later at the end of training camp. We obtained written informed
consent that was approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board (#2018-684)
and the study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association,
2013).
Participants
A sample of convenience of 75 adult American style football players were recruited from
a group of players enrolled in a specialised training camp at a local performance centre
for the 2024 NFL draft. Players represented a variety of field positions (e.g., wide
receivers, tight ends, defensive linemen) and had competed for different university

Introduction
Sprint speed is a key skill for American style football players. Players seeking to be drafted
by the National Football League (NFL) showcase their linear speed running abilities in
the 36.6 m (40 yard) dash at an annual combine. The combine is a weeklong invitation-
only event where top university prospects (approximately 300) perform physical and
mental assessments for personnel of the league’s 32 teams. Research shows drafted
players perform better in the 36.6 m sprint than non-drafted players (Sierer et al.,
2008) and superior performance is associated with higher draft position (Tucker &
Black, 2023). Combine invitees and other eligible players attend specialised training
camps leading up to the NFL draft to prepare. Linear speed mechanics is one focus of
these camps since players must transition from game play running to test performance
running. Mokha et al. (2021) showed that 36.6 m time significantly improved in a group
of American style football players participating in a six-week NFL draft preparation
camp. Players appeared to accomplish this through decreasing ground contact time (pre,
177 ± 3.2 vs. post, 168 ± 2.2 ms) and increasing average vertical ground reaction force

(vGRF) (pre, 1.5 ± 0.3 vs. post, 1.6 ± 0.1 BW). These changes represent hallmarks of
higher velocity runs (Colyer et al., 2018; Morin et al., 2011; Weyand, 2017; Weyand et al.,
2010). While these changes alone would not be enough to improve the participants’
linear speed in the 36.6 m dash, they shed light on how foot-ground kinetics are modifi­
able in elite American style football players and provide foundation for further kinetic
analysis.
    During running, mechanical work must be done to rotate limb segments, restore
energy lost during early ground contact, and propel the body forward. Given that ground
contact times for sprinting range from 85 to 190 ms (Mattes et al., 2021; Numella et al.,
2007; Weyand et al., 2010), the ability to perform work in a short time is vital and gives
rise to examining joint power. Decrements in the capacity of the muscles to produce
adequate power during running have been shown to negatively impact sprint speed
(Sánchez-Sánchez et al., 2018; Small et al., 2009). Joint power is distinguished from
system power where system power represents the rate at which the mechanical work is
done on an external load and may veil the power contributions from the individual joints
(Moir et al., 2012). Joint powers represent the rate at which mechanical work is accom­
plished at the joints providing estimates of muscle activity (Pires et al., 2014; Riddick &
Kuo, 2022). Joint power magnitudes have been shown to increase as running speeds
increase (Belli et al., 2002; Khassetarash et al., 2020). While improvements in speed and
system power performance have been documented in American style football players
undergoing training (Crawley et al., 2024; Gillen et al., 2024; Hoffman et al., 2004, 2009;
Moore & Fry, 2007), the joint level mechanisms underlying adaptation have not been
explored.
    Positive joint power is primarily generated by concentric muscle contractions and
potential strain energy is released. Most of the positive power (>60%) is generated at the
ankle joint during ground contact when the plantar flexors (gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles) contract to propel the body forward (Swinnen et al., 2021). Sanno et al. (2018)
reported that prolonged running at near maximal effort shifted the distribution of
positive joint work proximally in recreational but not competitive distance runners
suggesting that shifting positive joint work from the ankle plantar flexors towards hip
extensors could be detrimental to running economy. This shift has also been reported to
occur in middle-distance runners completing an exhaustive run (181 ± 42 s to exhaus­
tion) and in older runners as a sign of performance decline (Kim & Park, 2022).
Furthermore, hip muscle activation during the swing phase consumes energy, leading
to the estimated relative contribution of leg swing to the energetic cost of 7–11%
(Swinnen et al., 2021). While these findings appear to indicate that a distal-to-proximal
shift may be deleterious, it may be a necessary adaptation to faster running speeds. For
example, the hip’s contribution to average positive power in both stance and swing
phases has been shown to significantly increase with faster running speeds (i.e.,
6.0–9.0 m/s) (Schache et al., 2011, 2015). AminiAghdam et al. (2021) found that anterior
trunk lean shifted power from the knee to the hip during level and uneven running at
speeds of 3.5 m/s.
    Negative joint work and power are primarily generated by eccentric muscle contrac­
tions where potential strain energy is stored and mechanical energy is reduced (DeVita et
al., 2007). Since eccentric muscle contractions are associated with greater muscle damage
(Hashizume et al., 2017), negative joint power is of particular interest. Negative power is
                                                                  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       3
produced during the braking phase of running and is controlled reflexively by the leg
extensors (Belli et al., 2002). The knee and ankle joints contribute greatly to limb power
absorption compared to the hip joint (Hashizume et al., 2018). Belli et al. (2002) found
the overall negative work absorbed at initial contact was lower than the positive power
produced at end contact point, especially at the knee joint. The elongation time of the
ankle and knee muscles is short and has been attributed to high ankle joint stiffness
preventing yielding of the centre of mass at initial contact (Belli et al., 2002). It is not
known how participating in a performance preparation program affects this mechanism.
   Magnitudes and percentage contributions of joint power to total limb power may be
sensitive to training aimed at improving linear speed mechanics even in highly trained
athletes. Exploring joint level mechanics in American style football players may provide
insight into the mechanistic adaptations of running performance that may carry over to
other team sports where running is integral such as rugby, football (soccer), or Australian
rules football. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to assess the changes in joint
power magnitude and distribution during a high-speed run before and after a six-week
training camp in American style football players. We hypothesised that speed focused
exercises presented in training camp would redistribute the power contributions from
the lower limb joints, characterised by a reduction of power from the ankle even if
treadmill speed were kept uniform. To test the hypothesis, we used an inverse dynamic
approach to calculate individual joint and total limb powers during a high-speed run
before and after participation in training camp.

Experimental approach
This study was part of a larger study monitoring pre-post changes in body composition,
and vertical jump and speed running mechanics over the duration of a six-week training
camp designed to prepare eligible American style football players for the NFL draft.
Camp was divided into three microcycles that included drill specificity training, player
position specificity training, resistance training and recovery-based movement (e.g.,
pool, soft tissue massage). The study procedures were conducted at the start of training
camp and six weeks later at the end of training camp. We obtained written informed
consent that was approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board (#2018-684)
and the study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association,
2013).

teams in the United States. All participants had just completed their collegiate football
season, were active players training 5-6× per week, and were cleared by licenced medical
staff to participate in the study. All 75 completed the testing, but 23 were excluded due to

speed. Previous studies have assessed joint power redistribution during fatiguing or
exhaustive runs (Melaro et al., 2021; Willer et al., 2021), changing stride mechanics
and/or speed (Belli et al., 2002; Dewald et al., 2023; Schache et al., 2011), between
recreational and competitive runners (Sanno et al., 2018), and in older runners (Kim &

and after a training block in highly skilled athletes. We hypothesised that participation in
training camp would redistribute both positive and negative joint power from the ankle
towards the more proximal hip joint and knee joints even if treadmill speed were kept
uniform between testing sessions. The hypothesis was partially accepted.

between testing sessions to aid in distinguishing camp participation effects on the
dependent variables. The joint power magnitudes in the current study are comparable
to those from similar speed runs in previous studies (Belli et al., 2002; Kariyama & Zushi,
2016) and show the ankle to be the dominant power producer bilaterally for both
absorption (~50%) and release (~65%) (Belli et al., 2002; Schache et al., 2015; Stearne
et al., 2014). Total positive power did not change for both limbs after training camp.

in the current study was 6.4 m/s and was the same for both testing sessions. Muscles
around the hip appear to have generated greater work during the propulsion phase
(Figure 6) just as occurs with running at faster speeds. This may be a marker of improved
limb efficiency. However, the effect sizes were small (left, r = .24; right, r = .20). Further,
not all participants increased positive hip joint power. Ten players (19%) decreased by 0.5
to 6.0 W/kg. A runner may become more reliant upon hip muscles if unable to generate
power through the calf muscles (van Oeveren et al., 2024). This has been shown to occur
when runners shift to a higher step frequency at a lower speed (van Oeveren et al., 2024)
which also lowers ground contact time. Subjects in the current study decreased their
ground contact times on the left side from 160 ms to 158 ms and maintained 158 ms on
the right side at both testing runs leading to symmetrical ground contact times. Limb

values show between the right and left ankles. During sprinting, the ankle joint plays
an important role in producing the necessary large vertical ground reaction force (vGRF)
(Dorn et al., 2012; Schache et al., 2014; Stefanyshyn & Nigg, 1998), reducing ground
contact time (Charalambous et al., 2002), and enhancing mechanical efficiency
(Kuitunen et al., 2002). Specifically, the ankle plantar flexor muscles (gastrocnemius
and soleus) have a dominant role in those tasks and rely greatly on the utilisation of
tendon elastic strain energy for generating power during the stance phase. In the current
study, mean stance-averaged vGRFs were unchanged for the left (pre, 18.39 ± 1.38 vs.
post, 18.47 ± 1.33 N/kg) and right (pre, 18.37 ± 1.78 vs. 18.28 ± 1.61 N/kg) limbs which

limb power (~47–51%) at both testing sessions was performed around the ankle joint.
Greater muscle damage occurs with cumulative negative work, or eccentric loads
(Hashizume et al., 2019). Thus, this finding was seen as not only potentially enhancing
for performance but also increasing injury protection. Further, ground contact times
have been found to be relatively consistent up to 20 km/hr and then may vary with lesser
skilled runners demonstrating an inability to generate high braking and propulsive forces
in a short time by the muscles. Participants increased hip and knee negative power during
braking period and increased hip positive power during propulsion. Enhancements in
swing leg mechanics, specifically ‘leg retraction’ may have influenced the findings for
negative joint power. Leg retraction is the rearward leg rotation before initial ground
contact and is controlled primarily by hip rotation (Orendurff et al., 2018) with the
extensors as prime forward movers of the body (Belli et al., 2002). Leg retraction
enhances running mechanics by reducing horizontal velocity difference of the foot
relative to the surface (Blazevich, 2017; Blum et al., 2010). This reduces impact impulse,
prevents slipping (Karssen et al., 2015), improves stability (Blum et al., 2010; Karssen et
al., 2011), and possibly decreases total limb negative power, specifically at the ankle.
Decreases in negative power have been shown to result from improved muscle-tendon
elasticity and stiffness (Hirayama et al., 2017; Kubo et al., 2010, 2012), stride mechanics
(Swinnen et al., 2021), and neuromuscular control (Akbar et al., 2022). Thus, this change
may be a training adaptation reflective of enhanced linear speed mechanics. However, all
players did not exhibit this shift. Seventeen (~33%) participants had 0.5 to 9 W/kg
increases in negative hip joint power and five (~10%) had ≥ 9 W/kg increases in negative
ankle joint power. Intervention programs of ≥12 weeks have been shown to be most
beneficial to muscle-tendon adaptation (Bohm et al., 2015; Hirayama et al., 2017) while
stride mechanics and neuromuscular control programs may induce beneficial changes in
performance in 2–8 weeks (Akbar et al., 2022; Barber-Westin et al., 2015; Maćkała &
Fostiak, 2015). Thus, it is plausible that the sprint technique drills, and the other related
camp exercises may have reduced the need of the ankle joint’s muscle-tendon complex
for energy absorption for most of the participants. To illustrate, the first five linear speed
drills in Table 1 focus on rapid ankle dorsiflexion at foot-off and piston-like motion at the
hips and knees. Improvements in force application mechanics may have aided in redis­
tributing joint power especially for players of positions where sprinting is required such
as offensive and defensive linemen. However, position differences were not evaluated in
the current study. This group began training camp with most participants just finishing
their competitive playing season where mechanics of game specific demands such as
changes of direction and large decelerations were predominant for most player positions.
The goal of training camp was to prepare participants for their professional try-out in
which they showcase linear speed in the 36.6 m run.
    The unique participant pool, elite-level American style football players training
for the NFL draft at a single facility presented an opportunity to monitor a highly
specialised sample but also made it difficult to utilise a control group. Without a
control group, we cannot be confident that the observations were solely from the
training camp protocol. Footwear differences between testing sessions, muscle
soreness, fatigue, energy intake, limb dominance, or previous injury may have
influenced the findings. However, it should be noted that training camp protocols
for resistance training, field-drills, sleep, nutritional supplements, recovery
 14      G. M. MOKHA ET AL.
treatment, corrective exercises, and injury management are strict and consistent
strengthening findings within pre-post test limitations. Furthermore, 43/52 (83%)
of the participants were categorised as Skill (e.g., wide receivers, defensive backs)
or Big-skill (e.g., tight ends, linebackers) who run the ball more in American style
football. The remaining were Big players (linemen) who primarily block and
tackle. Thus, the small to moderate r effect sizes observed may have been
influenced by player position.
Conclusion
This study is the first to longitudinally examine changes in joint-level power
magnitude and contribution during speed running before and after a training
block in a group of highly skilled athletes. The goal was to gain insight into joint-
specific mechanistic adaptations that would provide valuable information for what
is possible in high calibre team sport athletes attempting to enhance linear speed.
The primary generator of both positive and negative joint power was the ankle,
and this was consistent with previous findings (Swinnen et al., 2021). Positive
power contribution at the ankle decreased by ~ 0.5% and increased at the hip by ~
1.0%, but these were not significant. The interesting change was that of decreased
negative ankle power bilaterally indicating less reliance on the ankle’s muscle-
tendon complex for energy absorption during the first portion of the stance phase.
This change occurred despite running at the same speed (mean 6.4 m/s) before
and after training camp. The distal-to-proximal shift in negative joint power as a
by-product of training requires further investigation. Given that the high skill of
the participants may affect the sensitivity of change of the variables in this study,
the moderate and low effect sizes produced may still warrant attention. We also
observed individual differences in the training response that might have affected

power magnitude influenced this finding. Most of the power absorbed relative to the total
 12       G. M. MOKHA ET AL.
Figure 5. Relative contribution of the right ankle, knee, and hip to the total average positive and
negative joint power during the pre-test (top) and post-test (bottom). The radius of each pie chart is
scaled based on the total positive power of each condition.
Figure 6. Time series normalised to stance phase (100%) for left (top row) ankle (a), knee (b), and hip
(c) power and right (bottom row) ankle (d), knee (e), and hip (f) power for the pre-test and post-test.
                                                                  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        13
limb power (~47–51%) at both testing sessions was performed around the ankle joint.
Greater muscle damage occurs with cumulative negative work, or eccentric loads
(Hashizume et al., 2019). Thus, this finding was seen as not only potentially enhancing
for performance but also increasing injury protection. Further, ground contact times
have been found to be relatively consistent up to 20 km/hr and then may vary with lesser
skilled runners demonstrating an inability to generate high braking and propulsive forces
in a short time by the muscles. Participants increased hip and knee negative power during
braking period and increased hip positive power during propulsion. Enhancements in
swing leg mechanics, specifically ‘leg retraction’ may have influenced the findings for
negative joint power. Leg retraction is the rearward leg rotation before initial ground
contact and is controlled primarily by hip rotation (Orendurff et al., 2018) with the
extensors as prime forward movers of the body (Belli et al., 2002). Leg retraction
enhances running mechanics by reducing horizontal velocity difference of the foot
relative to the surface (Blazevich, 2017; Blum et al., 2010). This reduces impact impulse,
prevents slipping (Karssen et al., 2015), improves stability (Blum et al., 2010; Karssen et
al., 2011), and possibly decreases total limb negative power, specifically at the ankle.
Decreases in negative power have been shown to result from improved muscle-tendon
elasticity and stiffness (Hirayama et al., 2017; Kubo et al., 2010, 2012), stride mechanics
(Swinnen et al., 2021), and neuromuscular control (Akbar et al., 2022). Thus, this change
may be a training adaptation reflective of enhanced linear speed mechanics. However, all
players did not exhibit this shift. Seventeen (~33%) participants had 0.5 to 9 W/kg
increases in negative hip joint power and five (~10%) had ≥ 9 W/kg increases in negative
ankle joint power. Intervention programs of ≥12 weeks have been shown to be most
beneficial to muscle-tendon adaptation (Bohm et al., 2015; Hirayama et al., 2017) while
stride mechanics and neuromuscular control programs may induce beneficial changes in
performance in 2–8 weeks (Akbar et al., 2022; Barber-Westin et al., 2015; Maćkała &
Fostiak, 2015). Thus, it is plausible that the sprint technique drills, and the other related
camp exercises may have reduced the need of the ankle joint’s muscle-tendon complex
for energy absorption for most of the participants. To illustrate, the first five linear speed
drills in Table 1 focus on rapid ankle dorsiflexion at foot-off and piston-like motion at the
hips and knees. Improvements in force application mechanics may have aided in redis­
tributing joint power especially for players of positions where sprinting is required such
as offensive and defensive linemen. However, position differences were not evaluated in
the current study. This group began training camp with most participants just finishing
their competitive playing season where mechanics of game specific demands such as
changes of direction and large decelerations were predominant for most player positions.
The goal of training camp was to prepare participants for their professional try-out in
which they showcase linear speed in the 36.6 m run.
    The unique participant pool, elite-level American style football players training
for the NFL draft at a single facility presented an opportunity to monitor a highly
specialised sample but also made it difficult to utilise a control group. Without a
control group, we cannot be confident that the observations were solely from the
training camp protocol. Footwear differences between testing sessions, muscle
soreness, fatigue, energy intake, limb dominance, or previous injury may have
influenced the findings. However, it should be noted that training camp protocols
for resistance training, field-drills, sleep, nutritional supplements, recovery
 14      G. M. MOKHA ET AL.
treatment, corrective exercises, and injury management are strict and consistent
strengthening findings within pre-post test limitations. Furthermore, 43/52 (83%)
of the participants were categorised as Skill (e.g., wide receivers, defensive backs)
or Big-skill (e.g., tight ends, linebackers) who run the ball more in American style
football. The remaining were Big players (linemen) who primarily block and
tackle. Thus, the small to moderate r effect sizes observed may have been
influenced by player position.
Conclusion
This study is the first to longitudinally examine changes in joint-level power
magnitude and contribution during speed running before and after a training
block in a group of highly skilled athletes. The goal was to gain insight into joint-
specific mechanistic adaptations that would provide valuable information for what
is possible in high calibre team sport athletes attempting to enhance linear speed.
The primary generator of both positive and negative joint power was the ankle,
and this was consistent with previous findings (Swinnen et al., 2021). Positive
power contribution at the ankle decreased by ~ 0.5% and increased at the hip by ~
1.0%, but these were not significant. The interesting change was that of decreased
negative ankle power bilaterally indicating less reliance on the ankle’s muscle-
tendon complex for energy absorption during the first portion of the stance phase.
This change occurred despite running at the same speed (mean 6.4 m/s) before
and after training camp. The distal-to-proximal shift in negative joint power as a
by-product of training requires further investigation. Given that the high skill of
the participants may affect the sensitivity of change of the variables in this study,
the moderate and low effect sizes produced may still warrant attention. We also
observed individual differences in the training response that might have affected
